paragraphs.text: It is commonly thought that sports teams enjoy a big advantage whenever they play at home, and many supporters believe they have a direct impact on the outcome of home matches. marches. When their team plays poorly, we think it’s the fans’ fault for not getting behind them, and when their team plays well, it's the fans who can take the credit for defending ‘their territory’.

According to recent sports science studies, it appears that fans, players and the media have bought into a myth of their own relative power or powerlessness. There is little proof that match results are much affected by the size, intensity or commitment of the crowd. Instead, 'home advantage is remarkably consistent within sports across different locations and different crowds. Where it varies, the factors that count appear to be skill, luck and changes of circumstance.

When the English football team Arsenal moved stadium some years ago, they drew a large number of home matches against teams they would normally have expected to beat. This corresponds with a trend observed in the US, which shows that teams sacrifice home advantage for about six to nine months following a move, as the players adjust to their surroundings. This holds even when the move is from one anonymous modern sports arena to another, and even when, as in Arsenal's case, crowd capacity increases.

It could be argued that, since the move to a new stadium is equally traumatic for supporters, Arsenal's fans were the ones who took time to adjust, and it was only when they found their old voice that the team started to respond. But there is no evidence to back this up. It is easy for fans to confuse cause and effect, and to assume that their team only started playing well once they started cheering, rather than vice versa. There is one conventional fan's-eye view that does seem to be confirmed by scientific evidence, however. As well as trying to encourage the players, home fans direct much of their vocal effort at referees. Recent research suggests that they do so with good reason.

In one well-known experiment, 40 referees were shown a recording of a football match, half watching with crowd effects included and half watching a silent version. Those referees who heard the crowd were less likely to call fouls against the home team than those who saw the game in silence. Interestingly, however, the noise made them no more likely to penalise the away team. These decisions coincided with those of the official at the actual match. The researchers concluded that referees tended to avoid making decisions that would direct the home fans' fury at them, in order to shield themselves from the stress that comes with antagonising the crowd.

The exrent of home advantage varies depending on the sport and in some sports there appears to be no home advantage. Match results show that basketball is the US game were playing at home still counts for most. The US National Hockey League, however, has scen a 15 per cent decline in the dominance enjoyed by home sides. Meanwhile, US baseball remains the sport where home advantage is least significant. One explanation is that home advantage is primarily a team phenomenon, and baseball is largely about individual confrontations between batter and pitcher. Studies of individual sports, such as golf and tennis, provide no evidence of any home advantage. If anything, the reverse scems to be true. In a sport such as basketball, by contrast, success depends on how players interrelate and find each other on the court. If you feel comfortable with your location, you have a better chance of knowing where your teammates are.

Recent studies reveal that home advantage has declined in all sports over time, contrary to widespread belief. For instance, in the 1890s, the earliest years of English league football, home teams tended to win about 70 per cent of points, compared to 60 per cent today. One explanation could be that the first referces were by definition less experienced and therefore potentially more susceptible to crowd pressures than today's professional officials are. Another might be transport – getting to and from grounds used to be slow and uncomfortable, while today's top teams are transported in luxury. Local conditions were more likely to vary in the early years, whereas these days most teams know exactly what to expect, and the top grounds increasingly resemble one another. And yet, plausible as these explanations are, none of them fits the data.

These changes all happened in recent decades, as a result of big money being poured into the sport. Yet the significant drop in home advantage actually occurred between 1946 and 1949, following the Second World War. Men who went away to war came back to find that their old grounds no longer felt so much like home; meanwhile, the away grounds probably didn't feel so foreign, either. And although home advantage reasserted itself somewhat during the more parochial Rifties, Sixties and Seventies, for some reason it never reacquired its old significance.

As sport becomes increasingly globalised and professional, it is also becoming ever more predictable. We don't fully understand the forces behind home advantage, but one thing is clear – it still has a part to play.
